title: Episode 192: George H.W. Bush: The Youngest Aviator, Chichi Jima, and the Presidency (1941–1989)
description:
George Herbert Walker Bush lived an epic American life of quiet valor, aristocratic decency, and relentless public service. Postponing Yale on his eighteenth birthday following Pearl Harbor, Bush became the youngest combat aviator in the United States Navy. In September 1944, while bombing a fortified radio tower on the Japanese island of Chichi Jima, his TBM Avenger was engulfed in flames from anti-aircraft fire; Bush completed his bombing run, bailed out into the Pacific, and floated in a life raft for hours before being miraculously rescued by the submarine USS Finback, escaping the gruesome fate of fellow pilots captured on the island. Moving to West Texas with Barbara to build an independent oil fortune, Bush compiled the most distinguished resume in modern politics: Congressman, UN Ambassador, CIA Director, and Reagan's Vice President, before winning the presidency in 1988 under the banner of 'a thousand points of light.' Discover the humble heroism of America's forty-first president.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into the extraordinary, honorable world of George Herbert Walker Bush. Before he was president, '41' was a teenage combat pilot who survived being shot down in World War II, a Texas oil wildcatter, and the most versatile public servant of his generation. Here is George with the story of Chichi Jima, the oil patch, and the road to the White House.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE YOUNGEST PILOT IN THE NAVY
George Herbert Walker Bush was born in Milton, Massachusetts, in June 1924 into an elite, patrician New England family of profound civic responsibility and athletic prowess. His father, Prescott Bush, was a partner in Brown Brothers Harriman and later a respected United States Senator from Connecticut; his mother, Dorothy Walker Bush, was a formidable, devout woman who instilled in her sons an absolute horror of bragging or self-promotion, constantly admonishing them to put others first and practice modesty. In June 1942, on the day he graduated from the elite Phillips Academy in Andover, Massachusetts, eighteen-year-old George listened to the graduation address by Secretary of War Henry Stimson. Despite having been accepted into Yale, Bush walked straight into the Navy recruiting office on his eighteenth birthday. Enlisting as a seaman second class, he completed grueling flight training in ten months, receiving his naval aviator wings and an ensign's commission at age eighteen—the youngest commissioned combat pilot in the entire United States Navy. Enlisting on his eighteenth birthday demonstrated the deep patrician sense of noblesse oblige that defined the Bush family: privilege conferred a solemn duty to serve one's country in its hour of peril. His decision to enlist at eighteen set the pattern for a lifetime of public service, always choosing the path of duty over personal privilege. That youthful decision to serve his country set the tone for a life of selfless dedication to the highest ideals of American republican leadership.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: SHOT DOWN OVER CHICHI JIMA: SEPTEMBER 1944
Assigned to Torpedo Squadron 51 aboard the light aircraft carrier USS San Jacinto in the Pacific, Lieutenant Bush flew fifty-eight combat missions in his Grumman TBM Avenger, which he affectionately christened 'Barbara' after his teenage sweetheart. On the morning of September 2, 1944, Bush led a four-plane flight to bomb a heavily fortified Japanese radio and radar installation on the volcanic island of Chichi Jima, one hundred and fifty miles north of Iwo Jima. Diving through intense, black anti-aircraft fire, Bush's plane was struck by heavy flak; the engine exploded in roaring flames, filling the cockpit with thick, toxic smoke. Refusing to pull out of his dive, twenty-year-old Bush stayed on target, released four five-hundred-pound bombs directly onto the radio installation, and pulled out over the ocean before ordering his crew to bail out. Parachuting into the waves, Bush suffered a head laceration when he struck the horizontal stabilizer. Floating in a tiny yellow rubber life raft four miles offshore, Bush watched in terror as Japanese patrol boats set out from the island to capture him, paddling frantically with his hands while American fighter planes strafed the enemy boats to keep them at bay. The harrowing combat mission over Chichi Jima revealed the extraordinary valor of a twenty-year-old pilot who completed his bombing run while his aircraft was consumed by roaring flames. His courage in the skies over Chichi Jima exemplified the selfless heroism of the Greatest Generation, young men who risked everything to preserve democratic freedom. Floating in the vast expanse of the ocean, Bush drew upon a profound faith that sustained his courage through hours of peril.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE SUBMARINE RESCUE AND THE SECRET OF CHICHI JIMA
For three agonizing hours, Bush drifted alone under a scorching sun, vomiting from swallowed saltwater, weeping for his two lost crewmen, radioman John Delaney and gunner William White, who had perished in the crash. Suddenly, through his tears, he saw a black steel hull rise like a sea monster from the waves: the submarine USS Finback, which had surfaced right beside his raft. Looking up at the bearded submariners, Bush stammered: 'Happy to be aboard.' A sailor aboard the submarine captured the rescue on sixteen-millimeter color film—one of the most remarkable wartime footage reels in history. Unknown to Bush until decades later, his survival was an unbelievable miracle of fate: eight other American aviators shot down during the same raid were captured by Japanese troops on Chichi Jima, subjected to horrific torture, executed, and their livers cannibalized by Japanese officers. For thirty days, Bush served aboard the Finback as it patrolled submarine waters, awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross for his heroism, haunted for the rest of his life by a quiet, reverent question: 'Why was I spared, and what did God have in store for me?' That miraculous submarine rescue by the Finback forged in Bush an abiding sense of providential purpose, believing his life had been spared for a greater destiny of public service. That miraculous rescue at sea gave Bush an unshakeable inner serenity, viewing every subsequent day as an unearned gift to be spent in service to others.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: BARBARA, YALE, AND THE TEXAS OIL PATCH
Returning home in January 1945, Bush married eighteen-year-old Barbara Pierce in Rye, New York, beginning a magnificent, seventy-three-year love story that became the longest marriage in presidential history. Entering Yale University, Bush captained the varsity baseball team as a slick-fielding first baseman, leading the Bulldogs to the College World Series in 1947 and 1948, proudly meeting baseball legend Babe Ruth at home plate. Graduating Phi Beta Kappa with an economics degree in two and a half years, Bush made a bold, independent choice: rejecting comfortable Wall Street banking jobs, he packed his wife and baby son George W. into a red Studebaker and drove fifteen hundred miles to the sun-baked, dusty oil patch of Odessa, Texas. Starting out as a humble oilfield equipment clerk sweeping warehouse floors for Dresser Industries, Bush co-founded Zapata Petroleum in Midland, Texas, pioneering offshore drilling technology in the Gulf of Mexico and amassing an independent fortune through sheer grit, fair dealing, and mutual trust. The move to the Permian Basin proved Bush's independent spirit, building a thriving business from scratch through integrity, teamwork, and sweat rather than family connections. His success in the Texas oil business proved that integrity, fairness, and hard work are the truest foundations of entrepreneurial prosperity.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE PEERLESS RESUME OF PUBLIC SERVICE
Driven by his mother's ethos of selfless civic duty, Bush entered Texas politics, winning election to Congress from Houston in 1966. Over the next two decades, Bush compiled the most astonishing and varied resume in modern American statecraft. In 1971, President Nixon appointed him United States Ambassador to the United Nations, where Bush's warmth and diplomatic grace won friends across the globe. In 1973, in the depths of the Watergate scandal, Nixon asked Bush to chair the Republican National Committee; Bush preserved the party's integrity, eventually confronting Nixon directly and urging him to resign for the good of the nation. In 1974, President Ford appointed Bush Chief of the U.S. Liaison Office in Beijing, where George and Barbara rode bicycles through the streets of the Chinese capital, building personal ties with Chinese leaders. In 1976, Ford summoned Bush home to serve as Director of Central Intelligence, restoring morale and ethical standards to a demoralized CIA in the wake of congressional investigations. His extraordinary breadth of public service—from the halls of Congress and the United Nations to Beijing and the CIA—gave Bush an unrivaled preparation for the highest office in the land. Throughout his varied diplomatic and intelligence careers, Bush was revered by colleagues for his quiet discretion, modesty, and deep institutional loyalty.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE LOYAL VICE PRESIDENCY AND THE 1988 CAMPAIGN
In 1980, after challenging Ronald Reagan for the Republican presidential nomination in a spirited primary campaign, Bush accepted Reagan's invitation to become his vice presidential running mate. For eight years, Bush served as the quintessential loyal team player, traveling over one million miles to seventy-four countries, representing America at state funerals, and providing trusted, discreet counsel in the Oval Office without a single public leak or disagreement. When Reagan was shot in 1981, Bush deliberately refused to land his helicopter on the South Lawn, insisting that only the President should land on the White House grounds. In August 1988, accepting the Republican presidential nomination in New Orleans, Bush delivered the speech of his life, penned by Peggy Noonan: 'I want a kinder, and gentler nation.' He praised the power of voluntary community service as 'a thousand points of light,' and made an unyielding, fateful promise: 'Read my lips: no new taxes.' In November, Bush defeated Massachusetts Governor Michael Dukakis in a forty-state landslide, winning four hundred and twenty-six electoral votes. His eight years as Vice President established the gold standard of executive loyalty, providing discreet, dependable counsel to Ronald Reagan while representing the nation across the globe. His partnership with Ronald Reagan established a model of vice presidential loyalty, providing trusted counsel without ever seeking the public spotlight.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE 41ST PRESIDENT AT THE HELM
On January 20, 1989, sixty-four-year-old George Herbert Walker Bush took the oath of office as the forty-first President of the United States on the West Front of the Capitol. He was the first sitting vice president elected to the presidency since Martin Van Buren in 1836. In his inaugural address, Bush spoke with characteristic humility: 'We meet on democracy's front porch, a good place to talk as neighbors and friends... We have more will than wallet; but will is what we need.' He took command at the most perilous and turbulent geopolitical moment since the end of World War II: the Soviet empire was cracking at the seams, Eastern Europe was stirring with rebellion, and the post-war order was about to dissolve. With four decades of military, diplomatic, and executive experience, the quiet aviator from Chichi Jima stood ready to navigate the ship of state through a historic global transformation with steady, understated mastery. Taking the presidential oath in 1989, George H.W. Bush brought a lifetime of seasoned judgment and quiet modesty to the helm of a rapidly transforming world. President Bush brought an air of quiet dignity and seasoned statesmanship to the White House, navigating historic global changes with calm wisdom.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
George H.W. Bush reached the presidency through a lifetime of extraordinary personal heroism and humble public service. But his greatest tests lay immediately ahead on the world stage. Next week, we turn to the second half of the Bush presidency: his masterly handling of the fall of the Berlin Wall, the rapid triumph of Operation Desert Storm, his famous White House ban on broccoli that ignited a vegetable war, and the gracious farewell note left for Bill Clinton. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
